Sources and notes

Educational only, not medical advice. On a narrow screen, scroll the figure sideways. The zoom lines show which part of each panel is magnified, not by how much. The drawing is a schematic: outlines, sizes, cell numbers and positions are illustrative and nothing is to scale. The only numbers shown are the two percentages below.

  • Islets, about 1–2% of the organ. Islets of Langerhans are small structures within the exocrine tissue that account for only 1–2% of the entire organ: Röder et al., Exp Mol Med 2016 (PMID 26964835). Other reviews give other figures; one 2024 review states about 10% for the endocrine part, which we did not use.
  • Exocrine tissue, the rest. The ~98–99% is the remainder after the islet share (100% minus 1–2%), not a separate measurement, and it includes ducts and supporting tissue (vessels, nerves, connective tissue) as well as acini. I did not find a checked source that gives acini alone as a percentage, so no such number is shown.
  • Gross anatomy of the pancreas. Retroperitoneal position; head, neck, body and tail; head surrounded by the C loop of the duodenum; tail toward the splenic hilum; drainage through the main and accessory ducts into the duodenum: Talathi et al., Anatomy, Abdomen and Pelvis, Pancreas, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf NBK532912; PMID 30422507). The stomach is drawn, ghosted, only as an orientation aid.
  • Bile duct, ampulla and papilla. The common bile duct and pancreatic duct meet at the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater), which opens into the duodenum at the duodenal papilla under the sphincter of Oddi: Hundt et al., Anatomy, Abdomen and Pelvis: Biliary Ducts, StatPearls (NBK459246; PMID 29083810).
  • Position behind the stomach. The pancreas lies posterior to the stomach, separated only by the lesser sac: Mihoc et al., Biomedicines 2024 (full text, PMC11591934).
  • Histology. Pyramidal acinar cells around a narrow lumen; intercalated ducts continuing the acinar lumen and fusing into intralobular ducts, then interlobular and main ducts; main duct running from tail to head and gaining diameter as branches join it: Mihoc et al., Biomedicines 2024 (PMID 39595191; open text PMC11591934), used for these histology statements only.
  • Islet capillaries. The islet capillary network is denser than the exocrine one and its endothelium has more fenestrations (a review reports about ten times more): Zanone et al., Curr Diabetes Rev 2008 (PMID 18220689).
  • Human islet cell mix. Beta cells about half, alpha cells 33–46%, delta cells 8–12%, scattered through the human islet without anatomical subdivisions and most aligned along blood vessels, unlike the core and mantle of mouse islets; composition varies between islets (the drawing uses roughly 50/40/10): Cabrera et al., PNAS 2006 (PMID 16461897).
  • Acinar and duct cell function. Pandol, The Exocrine Pancreas, Morgan & Claypool Life Sciences 2010 (NCBI Bookshelf NBK54128); duct bicarbonate fluid: Lee et al., Physiol Rev 2012 (PMID 22298651).

Note on the percentages. Only the islet share (about 1–2%) is sourced. Acini alone are a smaller fraction than the whole exocrine compartment, so the bar labels the remainder as exocrine tissue, ducts and supporting tissue rather than giving a number for acini.

Simplified. One lobule and one islet stand for the gland; the islet in panel 2 and panel 3 is the same islet at two magnifications but its cells are not matched one to one. The islet is drawn too small in panel 2 and with far too few cells in panel 3; real islets hold many more (no count is given because none was verified here). Omitted: accessory duct of Santorini, centroacinar cells, nerves, lymphatics, the uncinate process, the portal and splenic veins, pancreatic polypeptide cells, and the islet's vessel hierarchy. The common bile duct is drawn over the head so both ducts are visible, though it runs behind it. The percentage bar is drawn, not measured. The papilla, ampulla and sphincter of Oddi are not labelled on the drawing; see Hundt et al. above. Moving dots (blue for juice, red for blood) are decorative flow, not rates.
